strengths: The paper addresses a highly relevant and timely challenge in discrete diffusion language models (DLMs): the trade-off between parallel token generation and local syntactic/semantic coherence.

The proposed CoDiLA framework is supported by solid theoretical analysis. Theorem 3.2 proves that block-level modeling strictly improves the lower bound on the NELBO, and Theorem 3.3 mathematically demonstrates that hard top-k truncation introduces an irreducible bias, justifying the necessity of the proposed soft-conditioning interface.

The hybrid architecture is highly elegant and practical: it retains the bidirectional capabilities and global drafting power of the DLM while delegating local sequence execution to a very compact auxiliary autoregressive (AR) model (0.6B parameters) within short, bounded blocks.

The empirical evaluation is thorough, showing a clear Pareto frontier improvement in both static and dynamic parallelism regimes across multiple competitive coding benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, EvalPlus, BigCodeBench).
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is focused exclusively on code generation. While code is an excellent testbed due to its strict structural syntax, validating CoDiLA on general-purpose natural language tasks would strengthen the generalizability of the findings.

The approach requires a separate finetuning step for the auxiliary AR model on SFT data. While the DLM itself is kept frozen, this training requirement adds complexity compared to entirely training-free decoding acceleration techniques.

The paper lacks a detailed breakdown of the memory overhead. Running both a 7B DLM and a 0.6B AR model concurrently in GPU memory is manageable, but concrete statistics on peak memory footprint during inference would be valuable for deployment considerations.

strengths: Solid theoretical foundations: The authors rigorously prove that block-level modeling reduces the lower bound of the negative evidence lower bound (NELBO) (Theorem 3.2), and show that soft-conditioning is necessary and sufficient to prevent irreducible bias from top-k truncation (Theorem 3.3).

Innovative hybrid design: Combining discrete diffusion for global planning with a lightweight autoregressive (AR) model restricted to short local blocks elegantly balances global parallel generation and local syntactic coherence.
Impressive empirical results: CoDiLA establishes a new Pareto frontier of accuracy and throughput on standard code benchmarks (such as HumanEval, MBPP, and BigCodeBench) over competitive baselines.
Excellent presentation and reproducibility: The paper is exceptionally well-written, with clear illustrative figures and highly detailed experimental configurations provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to code generation: Although code is a highly structured domain where local coherence is critical, assessing the method on general natural language datasets would demonstrate its broader applicability.

Brief analysis of the wall-clock latency overhead: A detailed breakdown of the time spent on DLM decoding, soft embedding projection, and AR generation would help clarify the exact computational bottlenecks.

Requires domain-specific training: The auxiliary AR model must be fine-tuned on the SFT dataset with block-level masking, which limits its plug-and-play capability for pre-trained DLMs on arbitrary domains.

strengths: Novel and elegant formulation that marries global parallel diffusion with local autoregressive refinement to preserve both global non-autoregressive capabilities and local syntactic coherence.

Strong theoretical foundation, including a proof that block-wise factorization strictly improves the NELBO lower bound (Theorem 3.2) and a proof that soft-conditioning is necessary to avoid excluding the global mode (Theorem 3.3).

Extensive empirical evaluation on challenging code generation benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, BigCodeBench) demonstrating a superior Pareto frontier of throughput vs. accuracy compared to strong baselines like ADJUST.
Insightful ablations, such as the comparison between soft-conditioning and hard Top-1 conditioning, which clearly validate the theoretical claims.
weaknesses: The assumption of fixed, non-overlapping blocks of size B may disrupt coherent structures that cross block boundaries. While the authors discuss this in the future work, it represents a notable limitation of the current design.

The throughput/latency is evaluated only at a batch size of 1. Because the method involves passing soft latents to an auxiliary 0.6B AR model at each step, the communication overhead and sequential decoding steps of the AR model could limit throughput scaling under larger batch sizes.
The auxiliary model (Qwen3-0.6B) is relatively large and requires end-to-end finetuning on 300k samples, representing a non-trivial training overhead compared to training-free verification methods.

Minor notation confusion: In Theorem 3.2, using B both as the block size and in the subscripts of B_1 and B_B (representing the NELBO bounds) is slightly confusing. Distinct notation would improve readability.

strengths: Well-motivated approach that directly addresses the conditional independence assumption in discrete diffusion models, which is a major bottleneck for their generation quality.

Solid theoretical foundation, with proofs demonstrating that block-level modeling reduces the negative ELBO compared to token-wise modeling, and that soft-conditioning avoids the irreducible bias introduced by top-K truncation.
Strong empirical results across various competitive code generation benchmarks, demonstrating a superior Pareto frontier of accuracy vs. throughput compared to prior work.
Versatility in preserving the native bidirectional and non-causal capabilities of DLMs, as demonstrated by the successful applications in infilling and planning tasks.
Comprehensive ablation studies that thoroughly validate design decisions such as boundary tokens, AR model scaling, and block unmasking strategies.
weaknesses: Increased system complexity: The framework requires managing and executing two models (a 7B DLM and an auxiliary 0.6B AR model) concurrently, which increases the memory footprint and implementation complexity.
Training overhead: Fine-tuning a separate AR model for each block size adds complexity and training overhead, making the pipeline less plug-and-play than standard parallel decoding strategies.

Dependence on vocabulary alignment: The soft-conditioning interface relies on vocabulary/tokenizer compatibility between the DLM and the auxiliary AR model. While the authors demonstrate that training a small AR model from scratch is possible for custom tokenizers, this could limit the direct usability of pretrained AR models when applying CoDiLA to arbitrary DLMs with different vocabularies.

strengths: The paper addresses a fundamental and well-known limitation of discrete diffusion language models (DLMs): the conditional token independence bias, which leads to local incoherence during parallel decoding.

The methodology is theoretically well-supported. Theorem 3.2 provides a formal proof that block-based factorization strictly reduces the lowest achievable negative evidence lower bound (NELBO) compared to token-wise factorization. Theorem 3.3 mathematically justifies the use of soft-conditioning over Top-K truncation, demonstrating that truncation introduces an irreducible bias that can exclude the global mode.

The soft-conditioning interface is elegant and highly practical. Mapping the DLM's full marginal probability distribution onto the AR model's token embedding space via an expected embedding allows the use of a lightweight, pretrained AR model without expensive alignment learning.

The empirical evaluation is highly comprehensive, spanning multiple code generation benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, BigCodeBench) and non-causal tasks (Infilling, ParallelBench, Graph Traversal). The proposed CoDiLA method consistently establishes a superior Pareto frontier for accuracy and latency relative to standard parallel decoding and direct competitors like ADJUST.
The paper is exceptionally well-written, with clear figures, detailed appendices, and rigorous ablation studies covering block size, AR model size, candidate scope, and batch size scaling.
weaknesses: The soft-conditioning approach relies heavily on tokenizer alignment. As detailed in Section A.1.2, Dream-Coder and Qwen3 share almost identical tokenizers. If the DLM and AR models used different vocabularies, a complex token-mapping or vocabulary translation layer would be required, limiting the plug-and-play nature of the method across arbitrary model pairs.

While CoDiLA significantly improves upon naive parallel decoding, there is still a noticeable performance gap between parallel decoding with CoDiLA and sequential decoding (K=1 baseline). For instance, on MBPP, sequential Dream-Coder achieves 80.5% Pass@1, whereas CoDiLA (Softmax, B=2) achieves 69.0%.

Deploying an auxiliary AR model alongside the DLM introduces additional system complexity and memory footprints. While the computational overhead of the 0.6B AR model is amortized at larger batch sizes (as shown in Table 8), there remains a throughput penalty at batch size 1, which is the most critical setting for low-latency interactive applications.

strengths: The paper is exceptionally well-motivated and theoretically grounded: Theorems 3.2 and 3.3 provide rigorous justifications for why block-level joint modeling reduces the negative ELBO (NELBO) and why soft-conditioning is mathematically superior to top-k truncation.

The proposed hybrid design is elegant and practical: by delegating local syntax resolution to a lightweight, soft-conditioned AR model while preserving the global bidirectional capabilities of the DLM, CoDiLA successfully addresses the local incoherence bottleneck of parallel decoding.
Strong empirical performance: CoDiLA establishes a new accuracy-latency Pareto frontier on code generation (HumanEval, MBPP, BigCodeBench) and planning tasks, reducing syntactic errors significantly.
Excellent and comprehensive ablations: The authors provide detailed experiments exploring block sizes, AR model scaling, candidate selection scopes, and multi-block generation.
weaknesses: Training overhead: The proposed framework requires fine-tuning the auxiliary AR model on the SFT dataset (and training a separate AR model for each block size), which limits the plug-and-play flexibility of the approach compared to training-free decoding methods.

Dependency on tokenizer alignment: The soft-conditioning interface relies on projecting the DLM's marginals onto the AR model's embedding space. While the authors show this is benign for Dream-Coder and Qwen3, adapting CoDiLA to models with completely different vocabularies may introduce additional alignment challenges.
